spans.assertion: tested whether referees are more likely to give red cards to dark-skinned than light-skinned players, using 106,803 player-referee dyads across four European leagues (2012-2013), via multivariable logistic regression with cluster-robust standard errors adjusting for games played, player position, league country, physical characteristics, and referee country implicit/explicit bias measures

the adjusted risk difference for dark- vs light-skinned players is +0.228 percentage points (95% CI -0.018 to 0.474; p=0.070), an 18.6% relative increase over the 1.22% baseline, narrowly missing significance at α=0.05
the adjusted odds ratio is 1.195 (95% CI 0.996-1.434; p=0.056), i.e. 19.5% higher odds of a red card for dark-skinned players

concluded the hypothesis receives marginal support: point estimates consistently favor the hypothesized effect and the 95% CI only barely includes zero, though it does not reach conventional significance
a sensitivity analysis treating skin tone as continuous found a statistically significant dose-response relationship (p=0.026), strengthening the case for an effect
reports the risk difference result in detail: point estimate 0.228 pp, 95% CI [-0.018, 0.474] pp, p=0.0699, SE=0.001256, not statistically significant at α=0.05

after adjustment, dark-skinned players have a 0.228 pp higher probability of a red card than light-skinned players (18.6% relative increase over the 1.22% baseline), with the CI barely including zero indicating substantial uncertainty
reports the odds ratio result in detail: OR=1.195, 95% CI [0.996, 1.434], p=0.0559, log-odds coefficient 0.1780 (SE=0.0931)
odds of a red card are 19.5% higher for dark-skinned players after adjustment, with the 95% CI barely including the null value of 1.0, consistent with the primary estimand

spans.note: Unit of Analysis and Sample Size subheading

spans.assertion: used the player-referee dyad as the unit of analysis
the sample comprises 106,803 dyads (89,535 light-skin [83.8%], 17,268 dark-skin [16.2%]) from 1,339 unique players and 2,816 unique referees
defined the outcome as a binary indicator of receiving any red card (1 or more) in the dyad
overall red-card prevalence was 1.26% (1,341/106,803): 1.22% for light skin, 1.42% for dark skin, an unadjusted risk difference of 0.202 pp
dichotomized skin tone into Light (0.00-0.25) vs Dark (0.75-1.00)
computed skin tone as the average of two independent raters' assessments on a 5-point scale
inter-rater reliability was r=0.923, described as excellent agreement
chose the light/dark dichotomization to create a clear distinction, excluding the ambiguous middle range (0.25-0.75)
adjusted the model for seven covariates: games played, player position, league country, player height, player weight, referee country mean IAT score, and referee country mean explicit bias score
excluded 38,422 dyads (26.3%) lacking skin tone data because players had no available photo for rating
excluded 17,015 dyads with medium skin tone (0.25-0.75) to create a clear contrast between light and dark categories
excluded 803 dyads (0.7%) with missing covariates, primarily missing height, weight, or bias measures
used logistic regression for the binary outcome
estimated the model via maximum likelihood
used cluster-robust (Huber-White) standard errors clustered by player to account for within-player correlation across referees
calculated the risk difference as average marginal effects via the delta method, comparing predicted red-card probability under dark vs light skin at observed covariate values
used Python 3.11 and statsmodels 0.14 (logit function with cluster covariance) as the software
the model achieved log-likelihood -6,701.3, pseudo R-squared 0.0696, and converged successfully after 171 iterations
in a model without referee-bias adjustment, the adjusted OR was 1.194 [0.995,1.433], p=0.057, virtually identical to the main analysis, indicating robustness to inclusion of bias measures

treating skin tone as continuous, the adjusted OR was 1.282 [1.030,1.598], p=0.026, a statistically significant dose-response relationship where each unit increase in skin tone rating raises red-card odds by 28.2%, supporting the hypothesis with a gradient effect
a median-split dichotomization (median=0.25, identical to the main cutoff) produced results identical to the main analysis

concluded the continuous-skin-tone analysis provides stronger evidence for the hypothesis, suggesting the conservative light/dark dichotomization may underestimate the relationship, since the significant gradient effect (p=0.026) shows red-card probability rising dose-dependently with skin tone
games played had OR=1.140 per additional game (p<0.001), each game increasing red-card odds by 14%, confirming an exposure effect
relative to defenders (baseline, most red cards), forwards (OR=0.640, p<0.001), goalkeepers (OR=0.708, p=0.008), and midfielders (OR=0.665, p<0.001) all had fewer red cards
relative to England (baseline), France (OR=1.614, p<0.001) and Spain (OR=1.660, p<0.001) had more red cards, while Germany (OR=0.868, p=0.133) was similar to England
referee-country implicit bias (IAT score) had β=3.971 (p=0.001), indicating higher implicit bias predicts more red cards
referee-country explicit bias had β=-0.556 (p=0.003), indicating higher explicit warmth toward whites predicts fewer red cards

assumed a logistic link function for the binary outcome and linear effects for continuous covariates

self-assessed the model-specification assumption as reasonable, noting the linearity assumption may be violated for games played (potential saturation) but sensitivity to transformations is likely minimal
self-assessed the positivity assumption as met, since both light and dark skin tones are represented across all positions, leagues, and referee countries
addressed the independent-observations assumption via cluster-robust standard errors clustered by player (1,339 clusters), accounting for multiple dyads per player
considered clustering standard errors by referee instead, but chose player clustering as more conservative given larger within-player correlation
self-assessed measurement validity as reasonable given high inter-rater reliability (r=0.923), while noting static photos may differ from in-game perception but likely correlate highly
assessed that missing skin-tone data more likely reflects club/league data practices than systematic differences among players without photos, limiting selection-bias concern

spans.assertion: summarizes the final inference: primary risk-difference estimand p=0.070 with 95% CI [-0.018,0.474] pp, positive direction, small but non-trivial magnitude (0.228 pp / 18.6% relative increase), CI barely including zero, and a significant continuous-skin-tone sensitivity result (p=0.026)
concluded overall that the hypothesis receives marginal but not conclusive support

the data suggest a small positive effect but with enough uncertainty that the null cannot be definitively rejected at α=0.05, though the p=0.070 result is close to threshold and the continuous analysis (p=0.026) provides stronger evidence, making the pattern more consistent with a small true effect than no effect
argues the 0.228 pp increase could be practically meaningful given its cumulative impact, red-card career consequences, and broader social implications of officiating bias

recommends future investigation with larger samples/meta-analysis, more granular per-match data, direct measures of player behavior/fouls, and experimental designs — none of which were carried out in this analysis
concludes the analysis provides suggestive but not definitive evidence of referee bias against dark-skinned players, with the balance of evidence leaning slightly in favor of the hypothesis
